canonical_statement: The study evaluated whether early goal-directed therapy initiated before ICU admission improved outcomes in patients with severe sepsis or septic shock.
This was a prospective randomized trial conducted in the emergency department of an 850-bed academic tertiary-care hospital from March 1997 through March 2000.
The intention-to-treat population comprised 263 randomized adults: 133 assigned to standard therapy and 130 assigned to early goal-directed therapy.

population.label: Adults with severe sepsis, septic shock, or sepsis syndrome enrolled in the emergency department

canonical_statement: Inclusion required at least two systemic inflammatory response syndrome criteria plus systolic blood pressure no higher than 90 mm Hg after a 20-30 mL/kg crystalloid challenge, or blood lactate at least 4 mmol/L.

population.label: Eligible emergency-department adults
inclusion_criteria: Systolic blood pressure <=90 mm Hg after 20-30 mL/kg crystalloid challenge over 30 minutes OR lactate >=4 mmol/L

canonical_statement: Major exclusions included age under 18 years, pregnancy, several acute competing diagnoses, contraindication to central venous catheterization, immediate surgery, active chemotherapy for uncured cancer, specified immunosuppression, do-not-resuscitate status, or directives restricting protocol implementation.

population.label: Screened emergency-department patients
exclusion_criteria: Acute cerebral vascular event or acute coronary syndrome
Acute pulmonary edema or status asthmaticus
Active gastrointestinal hemorrhage, seizure, drug overdose, burn injury, or trauma
Do-not-resuscitate status or restrictive advanced directives

canonical_statement: Randomization used computer-generated blocks of two to eight, with assignments concealed in sealed opaque randomly assorted envelopes opened by a hospital staff member who was not a study investigator.
Critical-care clinicians who assumed inpatient care were unaware of study-group assignment, and the study investigators did not influence ICU care.

Patients assigned to early goal-directed therapy received continuous central venous oxygen saturation monitoring and a protocolized resuscitation strategy in the emergency department for at least six hours.

exposures.duration: at least 6 hours in the emergency department

canonical_statement: Patients assigned to standard therapy received arterial and central venous catheterization and clinician-directed hemodynamic support with critical-care consultation before inpatient admission.

exposures.details: Clinician-directed hemodynamic support in the emergency department

canonical_statement: The early goal-directed therapy protocol used 500-mL crystalloid boluses every 30 minutes to target a central venous pressure of 8-12 mm Hg.

exposures.details: Target CVP 8-12 mm Hg

canonical_statement: If mean arterial pressure was below 65 mm Hg, vasopressors were used to maintain at least 65 mm Hg; if it exceeded 90 mm Hg, vasodilators were used until it was 90 mm Hg or lower.

exposures.details: Vasopressors for MAP <65 mm Hg; vasodilators for MAP >90 mm Hg

canonical_statement: If central venous oxygen saturation remained below 70%, red cells were transfused to achieve a hematocrit of at least 30%.

exposures.details: Used for ScvO2 <70% to target hematocrit >=30%

canonical_statement: After central venous pressure, mean arterial pressure, and hematocrit were optimized, persistent central venous oxygen saturation below 70% triggered dobutamine beginning at 2.5 micrograms/kg/min and increasing by 2.5 micrograms/kg/min every 30 minutes to a maximum of 20 micrograms/kg/min.

exposures.details: Maximum 20 micrograms/kg/min for persistent ScvO2 <70% after other targets optimized

canonical_statement: Patients in whom hemodynamic optimization could not be achieved received mechanical ventilation and sedatives to decrease oxygen consumption.

exposures.details: Fallback when hemodynamic optimization was not achieved

canonical_statement: In-hospital mortality was the primary efficacy end point.
Secondary end points included resuscitation end points, organ-dysfunction scores, coagulation variables, administered treatments, and health-care resource use.

outcome.definition: Resuscitation end points, organ-dysfunction scores, coagulation variables, administered treatments, and resource use

canonical_statement: The planned sample size was 260 patients to detect a 15-percentage-point reduction in in-hospital mortality with 80% power and a two-sided type I error rate of 5%, allowing for 10% refusal or exclusion.
Mortality was summarized with Kaplan-Meier estimates, risk ratios, and 95% confidence intervals; mixed models assessed prespecified secondary variables from 7 to 72 hours.
Two interim analyses were reviewed by an independent monitoring committee, and a DeMets-Lan alpha-spending approach set statistical significance at P<=0.04.
All 263 randomized patients were included in the intention-to-treat analyses.
The randomized groups did not differ significantly in baseline characteristics, including adequacy and duration of antibiotic therapy, or in baseline physiologic and organ-dysfunction measures.
Mean emergency-department stay was longer with early goal-directed therapy than with standard therapy (8.0 vs 6.3 hours, P<0.001).

canonical_statement: The authors described the study as an open, randomized, partially blinded trial with unavoidable interactions during the initial treatment period.
The authors noted that standard-therapy patients may have received some form of goal-directed therapy as the study progressed, potentially reducing the apparent treatment effect.
The authors noted a slight potential bias from investigators directly influencing care of patients in the early goal-directed therapy group during the initial treatment period.

The authors concluded that goal-directed therapy delivered at the earliest stages of severe sepsis and septic shock produced significant short- and long-term benefits by identifying high-risk patients early and restoring balance between oxygen delivery and demand.
